question:
The following sentence has been divided into four parts. Identify the part that contains an error.
(A) It is sad / (B) that you / (C) are believing / (D) in superstitious rituals.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (C) are believing.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "believe" is a stative verb (a verb of mental state/perception), and stative verbs are not used in the continuous/progressive (-ing) form in standard English.

• Rule — Stative Verbs: Verbs that express a state, feeling, possession, or mental process (e.g., believe, know, understand, want, love, hate, belong, seem) are normally used only in simple tenses, not in continuous tenses.

• In part (C), "are believing" must be corrected to "believe" — since the subject "you" takes a plural verb, the correct simple present form is "believe", not the continuous form.
◦ Corrected sentence: It is sad that you believe in superstitious rituals.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (A): "It is sad" — This part is grammatically correct; it correctly introduces the sentence with the impersonal subject "it".

• Option 3 (B): "that you" — This part is correct; "that" correctly introduces the noun clause and "you" is the subject of that clause.

• Option 4 (D): "in superstitious rituals" — This part is correct; "in" is the appropriate preposition to go with "believe" and "superstitious rituals" is correctly formed.

NOTE

• Other common stative verbs frequently tested by SSC: know, understand, believe, belong, prefer, seem, appear, possess, resemble, contain, consist, own, doubt, suppose.

• Some verbs (e.g., think, have, see) can be used in continuous form only when they express an action rather than a state — e.g., "I am thinking about it" (action) vs. "I think you are right" (state/opinion).

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
Since childhood, Monty / ate his food / fast and he / will not change.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. ate his food.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "Since childhood" indicates an action that began in the past and continues up to the present — this is a clear signal for the Present Perfect Continuous Tense, not the Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Since/For with Present Perfect (Continuous): When a sentence contains "since + a point of time" (e.g., since childhood, since 2010, since Monday) and the action is still ongoing, the verb must be in the present perfect / present perfect continuous form: has/have + been + V-ing.

• The segment "ate his food" (Simple Past) is therefore incorrect; it should be corrected to "has been eating his food".
◦ Corrected sentence: Since childhood, Monty has been eating his food fast and he will not change.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "fast and he" is grammatically correct; "fast" correctly functions as an adverb modifying the verb, and "and he" correctly joins the second clause.

• Option 3: "Since childhood, Monty" is correct; it correctly sets up the time-clause with the subject.

• Option 4: "will not change" is correct; the simple future tense is appropriately used here to express a habitual trait continuing into the future.

NOTE

• Other common time-markers that require the present perfect (continuous): since, for, so far, up till now, till date, lately, of late, this is the first/second time.

• Do not confuse "since" (point of time — since 2015, since Monday) with "for" (duration of time — for five years, for two hours).

question:
The following sentence has been divided into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
After your insistence, / my sister / checked / a mailbox again.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. a mailbox again.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "again" signals that the mailbox being referred to has already been mentioned or is known/specific from the context (it is being checked once more) — this calls for the definite article "the", not the indefinite article "a".

• Rule — Articles: The indefinite article "a/an" is used for a non-specific, first-time reference, while the definite article "the" is used when the noun refers to a particular, already-identified thing — signalled here by the repetition word "again".

• The segment should therefore read "the mailbox again" instead of "a mailbox again".
◦ Corrected sentence: After your insistence, my sister checked the mailbox again.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "After your insistence," is correct; it is a properly formed prepositional phrase acting as an introductory adverbial.

• Option 3: "my sister" is correct; it is a properly formed subject of the sentence.

• Option 4: "checked" is correct; it is the correct simple past tense form of the verb "check", agreeing with the past time frame of the sentence.

NOTE

• Words like again, once more, back, previously mentioned usually point to a specific/definite noun and therefore require "the".

• Commonly confused article errors on SSC exams also involve superlatives (always take "the"), unique objects (the sun, the moon), and first mentions (which take "a/an").

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
In order to connect / these themes to a wider / historical context, Rahul go / beyond aesthetic analysis.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. historical context, Rahul go.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject of the sentence is "Rahul", a third-person singular subject, so the main verb must take the singular form "goes", not the base form "go".

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement: A third-person singular subject (he/she/it/a singular proper noun) in the Simple Present Tense must be followed by a verb ending in -s/-es.

• The segment "Rahul go" is therefore incorrect and must be corrected to "Rahul goes".
◦ Corrected sentence: In order to connect these themes to a wider historical context, Rahul goes beyond aesthetic analysis.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "In order to connect" is correct; it is a properly formed infinitive phrase of purpose.

• Option 2: "beyond aesthetic analysis" is correct; it is a correctly formed prepositional phrase.

• Option 3: "these themes to a wider" is correct; it is a grammatically sound noun phrase functioning as the object of "connect".

NOTE

• Third-person singular subjects always require an -s/-es ending on the main verb in the Simple Present Tense: he goes, she runs, it works, Rahul studies.

• Watch for sentences with long intervening phrases (like "to a wider historical context") that separate the subject from the verb — this is a common SSC trick to obscure subject-verb agreement errors.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

There is nothing more (1)__________ than when you sit down at your table to study with the most sincere of intentions and instead of being able to finish the task at hand you find your thoughts (2)__________. However, there are certain techniques that you can use to (3)______ your concentration. To begin with, one should (4)______ to create the physical environment that is conducive to (5)_____ thought.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 1
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. frustrating.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage describes a person sitting down with sincere intentions to study but being unable to finish the task, and instead finding their thoughts wandering — this describes a negative, exasperating experience, which is best captured by the word "frustrating".

• Contextual clue: The sentence structure **"There is nothing more ___ than..."** is a comparative expression used to emphasise an extreme negative feeling, which fits "frustrating" (causing a feeling of dissatisfaction/annoyance from being unable to achieve something).

• The rest of the passage (mentioning "certain techniques" needed to fix the problem) confirms that blank 1 describes a problem/negative experience, consistent with "frustrating".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "exciting" is incorrect; it describes a positive feeling, which contradicts the negative tone of not being able to finish the task.

• Option 3: "interesting" is incorrect; it also carries a positive connotation that does not fit the context of struggling to concentrate.

• Option 4: "surprising" is incorrect; the situation described (mind wandering while studying) is a common, expected frustration, not something unexpected/surprising.

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always read the whole passage first to grasp the overall tone (positive/negative) before choosing an option for each blank — this passage has a clearly negative tone about difficulty concentrating.

• Similar "extreme feeling" comparative structures often tested: "There is nothing more annoying/irritating/discouraging than...".

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

There is nothing more (1)__________ than when you sit down at your table to study with the most sincere of intentions and instead of being able to finish the task at hand you find your thoughts (2)__________. However, there are certain techniques that you can use to (3)______ your concentration. To begin with, one should (4)______ to create the physical environment that is conducive to (5)_____ thought.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. wandering.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes being unable to finish the study task and instead finding one's thoughts drifting away from the subject — this is precisely described by the word "wandering" (moving aimlessly, straying from the point).

• Contextual clue: The verb "find" followed by **"your thoughts ___"** requires a word describing what the thoughts are doing — "wandering" correctly completes the idea of a distracted, unfocused mind.

• This also logically connects to the next sentence, which talks about techniques to improve concentration — confirming that blank 2 must describe a lack of focus.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "interesting" is incorrect; an adjective describing the thoughts as "interesting" does not logically connect to the need for techniques to improve concentration.

• Option 3: "tiring" is incorrect; it describes physical/mental exhaustion, not the specific problem of thoughts drifting away from the task.

• Option 4: "worrying" is incorrect; it suggests anxiety rather than the described problem of a lack of focus/distraction.

NOTE

• "Wandering" (of thoughts/mind/eyes) is a commonly tested word in SSC vocabulary and cloze passages, meaning to move without a fixed course or purpose.

• Related expressions: "wandering mind", "mind wanders off", "let one's thoughts wander".

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

There is nothing more (1)__________ than when you sit down at your table to study with the most sincere of intentions and instead of being able to finish the task at hand you find your thoughts (2)__________. However, there are certain techniques that you can use to (3)______ your concentration. To begin with, one should (4)______ to create the physical environment that is conducive to (5)_____ thought.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. enhance.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage talks about **"certain techniques that you can use to ___ your concentration" — since the passage is offering solutions to the earlier-described problem (a wandering, frustrated mind), the missing word must mean "to improve/increase", which is precisely the meaning of "enhance"**.

• Contextual clue: "Enhance" means to intensify, increase, or further improve the quality/value of something — here, one's concentration.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "commit" is incorrect; "commit your concentration" is not idiomatic English and does not fit the meaning of improving focus.

• Option 3: "discover" is incorrect; you cannot "discover" your concentration — this word does not fit the context of improving an existing ability.

• Option 4: "convince" is incorrect; "convince" means to persuade, which does not logically combine with "concentration" as its object.

NOTE

• "Enhance" is a frequently tested SSC vocabulary word; common collocations include enhance performance, enhance skills, enhance productivity, enhance concentration.

• Similar words meaning "to improve": improve, boost, strengthen, sharpen, augment.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

There is nothing more (1)__________ than when you sit down at your table to study with the most sincere of intentions and instead of being able to finish the task at hand you find your thoughts (2)__________. However, there are certain techniques that you can use to (3)______ your concentration. To begin with, one should (4)______ to create the physical environment that is conducive to (5)_____ thought.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. attempt.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads **"To begin with, one should ___ to create the physical environment that is conducive to..." — the structure "should ___ to + verb" requires a word meaning "try/make an effort", which is exactly the meaning of "attempt"**.

• Contextual clue: "Attempt to create" is a natural collocation meaning "to make an effort/try to create", fitting the advice-giving tone of the passage (suggesting the first step someone should take).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "imagine" is incorrect; "imagine to create" is not grammatically or idiomatically correct (imagine is normally followed by a gerund, not "to + infinitive", and its meaning does not fit here).

• Option 3: "announce" is incorrect; "announce to create" does not make logical sense in the context of personal study habits.

• Option 4: "lead" is incorrect; "lead to create" is not idiomatic, and "lead" does not fit the meaning of making a personal effort.

NOTE

• "Attempt to + verb" is a standard construction meaning "try to do something"; contrast with "imagine + gerund" (e.g., "imagine creating"), which is the grammatically correct form for "imagine".

• Other advice-giving structures common in SSC cloze passages: "one should try to...", "one ought to...", "it is advisable to...".

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

There is nothing more (1)__________ than when you sit down at your table to study with the most sincere of intentions and instead of being able to finish the task at hand you find your thoughts (2)__________. However, there are certain techniques that you can use to (3)______ your concentration. To begin with, one should (4)______ to create the physical environment that is conducive to (5)_____ thought.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. focussed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads **"...to create the physical environment that is conducive to ___ thought" — since the passage is about improving concentration, the missing word must describe a state of being concentrated/undistracted, which is exactly the meaning of "focussed"** (concentrated, attentive).

• Contextual clue: "Conducive to" means "making a certain situation likely or possible"; a good physical environment is conducive to focussed (concentrated) thinking, which directly supports the passage's central theme of improving concentration.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "joyful" is incorrect; a pleasant/happy state of mind is not the specific quality being discussed — the passage is about concentration, not happiness.

• Option 3: "cautious" is incorrect; being careful/wary does not fit the context of an environment meant to support studying.

• Option 4: "dazzling" is incorrect; this means "extremely impressive/bright", which has no logical connection to a state of thought suitable for studying.

NOTE

• "Focussed" (British spelling; "focused" in American English) is commonly tested in cloze passages relating to concentration and study habits.

• Words that collocate with "conducive to": conducive to growth, conducive to learning, conducive to health, conducive to concentration.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom in the following sentence.
Manish told Rounak time and again of the ill consequences of his habit of being late to the college.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Repeatedly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Time and again" means repeatedly, on many occasions, over and over again. (बार-बार)
◦ Example: The teacher warned the students time and again about the importance of punctuality.

• In the given sentence, Manish is described as having told Rounak about the consequences of lateness on numerous occasions, which matches the meaning of "repeatedly".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Hardly ever (शायद ही कभी): This means "almost never", which is the opposite of the intended meaning.

• Option 3: At intervals (रुक-रुक कर/कुछ अंतराल पर): This means occurring occasionally with gaps in between, which is weaker than the sense of constant repetition conveyed by "time and again".

• Option 4: Not often (शायद ही/कम ही): This also conveys infrequency, which is contrary to the idiom's actual meaning of frequent repetition.

NOTE

• Other idioms/phrases expressing frequency often asked in SSC: "Day in and day out" (every day without fail), "Over and over" (repeatedly), "Once in a blue moon" (very rarely).

• Do not confuse "time and again" (frequent repetition) with "once in a while" (occasionally) — they are near opposites.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Seema has a dominating nature, so she wants to ____________ of everything in her life.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. keep control.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "keep control of" means to have power over, or to be in charge of, something. (नियंत्रण रखना/काबू में रखना)
◦ Example: A good manager knows how to keep control of a difficult situation.

• Since Seema has a "dominating nature", it logically follows that she wants to be in charge of / have power over everything in her life — this is exactly the meaning of "keep control (of)".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "keep touch" is incorrect; the correct idiomatic phrase is "keep in touch (with)", meaning to stay in communication with someone — it does not fit the context of dominance.

• Option 2: "keep calm" is incorrect; this means to remain composed/relaxed, which does not match the idea of a dominating person wanting authority.

• Option 3: "keep record" is incorrect; the correct phrase is "keep a record (of)", meaning to maintain written information, which does not fit the sense of dominance described.

NOTE

• Common "keep" phrases tested by SSC: keep in touch (with), keep track (of), keep an eye (on), keep pace (with), keep watch (over), keep control (of).

• A "dominating" person typically seeks authority/control, which is the key contextual clue for this question.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
I am doubtful about his story, though you seem to be ________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. convinced.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "convinced" means fully persuaded or certain that something is true. (आश्वस्त/पूरी तरह विश्वास करने वाला)
◦ Example: After hearing all the evidence, the jury was convinced of his innocence.

• The sentence uses "though" to set up a contrast between the speaker (who is "doubtful") and "you" — the opposite of being doubtful is being certain/persuaded, i.e., "convinced".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "regretting" is incorrect; this means feeling sorry about something, which has no logical contrast with "doubtful" in this sentence.

• Option 2: "uncertain" is incorrect; this would mean "you" also lack confidence in the story, which is the same as being doubtful, not a contrast to it.

• Option 3: "pleasant" is incorrect; this describes a pleasing quality/manner, which does not logically contrast with "doubtful about a story".

NOTE

• The conjunction "though/although" always signals a contrast between two clauses — look for the word whose meaning is opposite to or different from the first clause.

• Word pair often tested: doubtful ↔ convinced/certain/sure.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Powerful
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Impotent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Powerful" means having great strength, influence, or authority. Its antonym, "Impotent", means lacking power, strength, or effectiveness; powerless. (शक्तिहीन/कमजोर)
◦ Example: The medicine proved impotent against the new strain of the virus.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Strong (शक्तिशाली): This is a synonym, not an antonym, of "powerful".

• Option 3: Manly (पुरुषोचित): This means having qualities traditionally associated with men, and is unrelated in meaning to a lack of power.

• Option 4: Wild (जंगली/उग्र): This means untamed or uncontrolled, which is unrelated to the concept of power or its absence.

NOTE

• Other antonym pairs of "powerful" often tested: powerful ↔ weak, feeble, helpless, frail.

• "Impotent" is also used specifically in medical/biological contexts, but in general vocabulary usage it simply means "lacking power or effect".

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
The government is planning to abolish child care leave for female employees.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Establish.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Abolish" means to formally put an end to a system, practice, or institution. Its antonym, "Establish", means to set up or bring into existence on a firm or permanent basis. (स्थापित करना)
◦ Example: The new law will establish a minimum wage for all workers.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Ensure (सुनिश्चित करना): This means to make certain that something happens; it does not carry the opposite sense of "creating/bringing into being" required here.

• Option 2: Eradicate (मिटाना/उन्मूलन करना): This is a synonym, not an antonym, of "abolish" — it also means to completely destroy or eliminate something.

• Option 3: Encourage (प्रोत्साहित करना): This means to give support or confidence to something/someone; it is not the direct opposite of "abolish".

NOTE

• Other words that are synonyms of "abolish" (often used as distractors): eliminate, eradicate, terminate, do away with, discontinue.

• Other antonyms of "abolish" that may be tested: institute, found, initiate, introduce.

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Definate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Definite", meaning clearly stated or decided; not vague or doubtful.
◦ Example: She gave a definite answer to the question.

• Spelling key: DEFIN + ITE. The word ends in "-ite", not "-ate". The given word "Definate" wrongly replaces the ending "-ite" with "-ate".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Appraisal" is spelt correctly; it means an assessment or evaluation of the worth of something.

• Option 3: "Stretch" is spelt correctly; it means to extend or be extended over an area.

• Option 4: "Genuine" is spelt correctly; it means truly what something is said to be; authentic.

NOTE

• The related word "definitely" is one of the most commonly misspelt words in English — remember it is "finite" (as in "finite/definite/infinite"), never "finate/definate/infinate".

• Other commonly confused "-ite/-ate" endings tested by SSC: opposite (not "opposate"), favourite (not "favourate").

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Estimate
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Evaluate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Estimate" means to roughly calculate or judge the value, number, quantity, or extent of something. "Evaluate" means to judge or calculate the quality, importance, amount, or value of something — the two words are close synonyms. (आकलन करना/मूल्यांकन करना)
◦ Example: The contractor was asked to estimate/evaluate the cost of the renovation.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Appropriate (उपयुक्त): This means suitable or fitting, and is unrelated to the act of judging value or quantity.

• Option 3: Profit (लाभ): This means a financial gain; it is a noun related to money, not a synonym of judging/calculating value.

• Option 4: Verify (सत्यापित करना): This means to confirm the truth or accuracy of something, which is different from making a rough calculation or judgement.

NOTE

• "Estimate" can function as both a verb (to estimate) and a noun (an estimate/a rough calculation).

• Other synonyms of "estimate": assess, gauge, appraise, reckon, calculate approximately.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
We shall rehearse thrice before the final performance at least we make errors in the dialogues.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. lest we make errors.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined segment "at least we make errors" is grammatically and logically incorrect in this context — the sentence needs a conjunction expressing "for fear that", which is the function of the word "lest".

• Rule — "Lest": "Lest" is a conjunction meaning "in order that ... not / for fear that", and it is followed by a clause using "should" or the subjunctive/simple form of the verb (e.g., "lest we make errors" = "so that we do not make errors").

• Applying this rule, the purpose of rehearsing thrice is to avoid making mistakes, which is correctly expressed as "lest we make errors" (for fear that we make errors).
◦ Corrected sentence: We shall rehearse thrice before the final performance lest we make errors in the dialogues.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "for we make errors" is incorrect; "for" (meaning "because") would illogically state that errors are the reason for rehearsing, rather than something to be avoided.

• Option 2: "but we make errors" is incorrect; "but" is a contrastive conjunction that does not fit the intended cautionary meaning.

• Option 3: "can we make errors" is incorrect; this forms an ungrammatical, question-like structure that does not fit as a subordinate clause here.

NOTE

• "Lest" is always used to express apprehension or a negative purpose — it inherently carries the meaning of "not", so it is never followed by another negative word like "not".

• Other purpose conjunctions commonly tested: "so that" (positive purpose), "in case" (precaution), "lest" (negative purpose/fear).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM for the underlined word in the given sentence.
Because the politician made a candid speech, he earned the respect of the voters.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Deceitful.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Candid" means truthful and straightforward; frank and honest, especially in situations where honesty might be uncomfortable. Its antonym, "Deceitful", means deliberately misleading or dishonest. (छलपूर्ण/धोखेबाज)
◦ Example: His deceitful promises fooled many voters before the election.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Reticent (मितभाषी/कम बोलने वाला): This means unwilling to reveal one's thoughts or reluctant to speak; while related to reserved communication, it is not the direct antonym of "candid" (honest).

• Option 2: Prudent (विवेकपूर्ण): This means acting with care and thought for the future; it is unrelated to honesty or deception.

• Option 4: Reckless (लापरवाह): This means acting without thinking about the consequences; it is unrelated to the concept of honesty.

NOTE

• "Candid" is frequently used in the phrase "to be candid with you", meaning "to speak honestly/frankly".

• Other synonyms of "candid" (often used as distractors): frank, forthright, sincere, straightforward; antonyms: deceitful, dishonest, evasive, insincere.

question:
Select the correct spelling of the underlined word in the given sentence.
She decided to file a complaint with HR after being harrasad by her supervisor for several weeks.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. harassed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Harassed", the past tense/past participle of "harass", meaning subjected to aggressive pressure or intimidation.
◦ Example: The employee reported that she had been harassed by a colleague.

• Spelling key: HAR + ASS + ED — one "r" and double "s". A common memory trick: "harass" has 1 r and 2 s's (opposite of "embarrass", which has 2 r's and 2 s's).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "harrassd" is incorrect; it has an extra "r" and is missing the "e" before the final "d".

• Option 3: "harrased" is incorrect; it has an extra "r" (double "r" instead of single) and only a single "s" instead of double "s".

• Option 4: "harased" is incorrect; it has only a single "r" and a single "s", missing one "s".

NOTE

• Remember: "harass" = 1 "r" + 2 "s"; "embarrass" = 2 "r" + 2 "s". Keeping these two commonly confused words distinct is a favourite SSC spelling trap.

• Related words: harassment (noun), harasser (noun), harassing (adjective/gerund).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word in the following sentence.
They studied during three hours.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. for.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — During vs. For: "During" is used before a noun denoting a period/event (e.g., during the holidays, during the meeting) to indicate when something happened, whereas "for" is used before a specific length/duration of time expressed as a number (e.g., for two hours, for three days) to indicate how long something happened.

• Since "three hours" is a specific numerical duration, the correct preposition is "for", not "during".
◦ Corrected sentence: They studied for three hours.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "by" is incorrect; "by" is used to indicate a deadline or point in time (e.g., "by five o'clock"), not a duration.

• Option 3: "at" is incorrect; "at" is used for a precise point in time (e.g., "at three o'clock"), not a span of duration.

• Option 4: "from" is incorrect; "from" indicates a starting point (often paired with "to"), not a standalone duration.

NOTE

• Quick rule: if the time expression can be preceded by a number (three hours, two weeks, five years), use "for"; if it names an event/period (the holidays, the war, the meeting), use "during".

• Similarly distinguished pair often tested: "since" (a starting point in time, e.g., since Monday) vs. "for" (a duration, e.g., for three days).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined words in the given sentence.
This newly arisen evidence could have proved to finally put the culprit behind bars.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. is proof.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "proved" cannot correctly take the infinitive "to finally put" as its complement in the intended sense — "proved to put" does not form a logically or grammatically sound expression, since "prove" is not used to mean "serve as a means of doing something".

• The intended meaning is that the evidence itself functions/serves as sufficient proof that can lead to the culprit finally being imprisoned — this sense is correctly expressed by the noun phrase "is proof", which pairs naturally with the following infinitive of purpose, "to finally put the culprit behind bars".
◦ Corrected sentence: This newly arisen evidence is proof to finally put the culprit behind bars.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "can proof" is incorrect; "proof" is a noun, not a verb, so it cannot follow the modal auxiliary "can" directly.

• Option 3: "can be proven" is incorrect; this passive form would mean the evidence itself needs to be established as true, which does not logically connect with the following infinitive "to finally put the culprit behind bars".

• Option 4: "could have been proven" is incorrect for the same reason as Option 3, and additionally implies a hypothetical/unfulfilled past possibility, which contradicts the sentence's intended meaning that the evidence is newly available and relevant now.

NOTE

• "Proof" (noun) vs. "prove" (verb) is a commonly confused word pair in SSC grammar questions — "proof" cannot be used as a verb.

• Watch for sentences where a verb is incorrectly followed by an infinitive that does not logically fit its meaning — substituting with the correct noun/verb form is a frequently tested error type.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Innovate
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Copy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Innovate" means to introduce new methods, ideas, or products; to make changes by introducing something original. Its antonym, "Copy", means to imitate or reproduce something that already exists, without creating anything new. (नकल करना)
◦ Example: Instead of innovating, the small company simply chose to copy its competitor's designs.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Solve (हल करना): This means to find an answer to a problem; it is unrelated to the concept of originality versus imitation.

• Option 2: Finance (वित्तपोषण करना): This means to provide funds for something; it is unrelated in meaning to "innovate".

• Option 3: Invent (आविष्कार करना): This is a synonym, not an antonym, of "innovate" — both involve creating something new.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "Invent" (a synonym distractor) with the actual antonym "Copy" — SSC frequently places a near-synonym among the options to test careful reading.

• Other antonym pairs on the same theme: original ↔ imitative; creative ↔ unoriginal; pioneer ↔ imitator.

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom to fill the blank in the given situation.
They were waiting for their family members who were returning from a pilgrimage. Therefore, they were ________________ on the platform.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. pacing up and down.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Pacing up and down" means walking back and forth repeatedly in a small area, typically out of nervousness, impatience, or anxious anticipation. (बेचैनी से इधर-उधर टहलना)
◦ Example: The nervous father was pacing up and down outside the delivery room.

• The situation describes people anxiously waiting on a platform for family members returning from a pilgrimage — a classic context in which people restlessly walk back and forth, matching this idiom exactly.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Running behind time" (देर होना): This means being late for something; it does not fit the description of restless waiting.

• Option 2: "Playing a joke" (मज़ाक करना): This means to tease or trick someone; it has no connection to anxious waiting.

• Option 4: "Rolling up their sleeves" (काम के लिए तैयार होना): This idiom means preparing to work hard/get down to a task; it does not fit the context of waiting on a platform.

NOTE

• Other idioms related to anxious waiting/restlessness often tested by SSC: "on tenterhooks" (in a state of suspense), "on pins and needles" (anxiously waiting).

• "Pacing" as a verb specifically refers to walking with slow, regular, and often repetitive steps, frequently used to describe nervous behaviour.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word.
The removal of petty restrictions has made life easier.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Small.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Petty" means of little importance; trivial or minor. "Small", in the sense of insignificant or minor, is its closest synonym among the given options. (छोटा/तुच्छ)
◦ Example: He was always fussing over petty/small details that did not really matter.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Big (बड़ा): This is an antonym, not a synonym, of "petty" — it means large or significant.

• Option 2: Consequential (महत्वपूर्ण): This means important or significant, which is the opposite sense of "petty" (trivial/unimportant).

• Option 3: Large (विशाल): This is also an antonym, referring to great size or extent, contrary to the meaning of "petty".

NOTE

• "Petty" is often used in phrases like "petty cash" (a small amount of money kept for minor expenses), "petty theft" (a minor crime), and "petty quarrels" (trivial disputes).

• Other synonyms of "petty": trivial, minor, insignificant, trifling, unimportant.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.
If you give away smoking, your health will improve.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. give up.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrasal verb "give up" means to stop doing something, especially a habit; to quit. (छोड़ना)
◦ Example: He finally decided to give up smoking after his doctor's warning.

• The underlined phrase "give away" means to donate or hand over something to someone else for free, which does not make sense in the context of "smoking" — one cannot "give away" a habit to another person. The intended meaning here is clearly to quit smoking, which requires "give up".
◦ Corrected sentence: If you give up smoking, your health will improve.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No substitution required" is incorrect because "give away" is factually and logically wrong in this context — a habit cannot be "given away" to someone else.

• Option 3: "give off" is incorrect; this phrasal verb means to emit or release something (e.g., a smell, heat, or gas), which does not fit the context of quitting a habit.

• Option 4: "give out" is incorrect; this phrasal verb means to distribute something or to become exhausted/stop functioning (e.g., "his strength gave out"), neither of which fits the context of quitting smoking.

NOTE

• Commonly confused "give" phrasal verbs tested by SSC: give up (quit/stop), give away (donate/reveal a secret), give off (emit), give out (distribute/run out/stop working), give in (surrender/yield).

• "Give up" can also mean "to surrender" in other contexts (e.g., "the criminal gave himself up to the police"), so context always determines the exact sense.
